title: The 1961 Phillips Device That Charged Without Wires—Executives Burned the Patent
hook: In 1961, Phillips demonstrated wireless charging decades before it was possible—then corporate executives burned the patent files to protect their wired empire.
why_this_can_go_viral: The idea that a major corporation deliberately burned the blueprint for wireless charging triggers outrage and 'what if' speculation, perfect for comment engagement.

title: The 4,800-Year-Old Sumerian Battery Found in Iraq—Smithsonian Refuses to Test
hook: A 4,800-year-old clay jar with a copper cylinder and iron rod produces electricity when filled with vinegar—but the Smithsonian refuses to run a single test.
why_this_can_go_viral: Ancient battery = instant curiosity. Refusal by major institution implies cover-up, fueling conspiracy theories and debate.

hook: In 1923, a French inventor built a car that ran purely on salt water—Renault bought the patent and demolished the factory the next week.

title: The 2,500-Year-Old Greek Robot That Served Wine—Then Vanished After a Feast

why_this_can_go_viral: Ancient robot story hooks viewers with 'how was this possible?' and the sudden disappearance creates mystery and shareability.

why_this_can_go_viral: Immortality is the ultimate curiosity trigger. The tragic deaths and government ban create a dark, emotional narrative arc.

title: The 1887 Belgian Light Bulb That Never Burned Out—Edison Bought and Destroyed It

why_this_can_go_viral: Edison is a famous 'villain' in suppressed-tech lore. The 40-year bulb story is widely shared; adding 'bought and destroyed' creates strong negative emotion.

why_this_can_go_viral: Antarctica mysteries are perennially viral. The specific year and NASA involvement add credibility, while 'data disappeared' triggers conspiracy interest.
